1.pericope_label: The congregation assembled, the sabbath renewed, and the offering called for

schools.summary: Gill dates the assembly from Jarchi to the day after Moses came down from the mount, the work having been held up by the golden calf and the making of reconciliation for it. He would render the first clause of the sabbath law may be done, every man being free to follow his calling on the six days unless the repetition looks particularly at the tabernacle and orders close work at it; and he takes the prohibition of fire for a temporary law, not said here as elsewhere to run throughout their generations but restrained to the season of the building, its purpose being to stop sabbath work on the tabernacle by leaving no fire to heat a tool or melt metal — for it can hardly be meant in the strictest sense, since fire is needful in cold weather and for infants, the aged and the sick. Calvin marks a change of grammar, that where the earlier passage used a verb this one uses a noun, willing of heart, though the sense is the same: God asks a cheerful zeal, so that they should give not only abundantly but gladly; and a further phrase follows for those whose heart stirred them up, setting them apart from the indifferent and the slow.

Henry reads the summons of all the congregation as a summons of the heads and rulers, who take their instructions from Moses as he took his from the Lord and pass them on to the people; and observes that Moses gave in charge all that God had commanded and no more, so proving faithful to both parties between whom he stood, though faithful as a servant only, where Christ was faithful as a Son. Of the sabbath he says that not a stroke was to be struck on it, not even at the tabernacle, the sabbath being the elder and more lasting honour, and offers two further renderings of the phrase — a sabbath of sabbaths, more excellent than any other feast and destined to outlast them all, and, as some of the Jews would have it, a sabbath and a little sabbath, since they add an hour at each end out of their own time to show how loth they are to part with it. On the offering he insists that it was no tax but a benevolence, which tells us that God has not made our yoke heavy, being a prince who does not burden his subjects but draws with the cords of a man, and that he loves a cheerful giver; and since the wise-hearted are called as well as the wealthy, he observes how variously God dispenses his gifts, the rich bringing materials and the skilful their skill, so that the tabernacle had need of both.

Wesley states the rule plainly, that the six days' work meant is work for the tabernacle, and restricts the prohibition of fire to servile work, a smith's or a plumber's, finding no evidence that it ever reached further. Clarke reports how the Jews themselves limit it, to fire kindled for work or for dressing food, holding it lawful to have light and heat — though they rarely kindle it, getting Christians to do that work for them; and he identifies the offering as a terumah, a heave-offering.

Ellicott approaches the law as legislation: the verse on the sabbath mainly repeats an earlier statute, but the verse forbidding fire is new, or at most implied before — and kindling fire was in those days hard manual labour, got by rubbing two dry sticks together.

7.pericope_label: The inventory of the work, and the people bring their offering

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the list is given again at all: having told them to supply the materials, Moses now calls for the industry that will shape and join them, and runs briefly over parts he had described at length before — the epitome being needed to spur them afresh, since instruction is often coldly received without exhortation. Asked where a pillaged people found such wealth, he answers that they must have been enriched at their departure by the booty God gave them, since what Egypt had heaped up by rapacity flowed away by God's secret influence when its people were made prodigal, and as he had blinded them into giving profusely, so he now inclined Israel to spend willingly what they had of his mere grace. He praises the premeditation of the gift, their departing from Moses' presence showing that they retired to their tents and considered by themselves what to give, since a man bountiful on sudden impulse often repents afterwards; and on the heart that stirred a man up he cautions that the Papists twist the phrase into a proof of free-will, whereas Moses in praising their spontaneity does not exclude the grace of the Spirit, who works within upon the will, so that believers stir up themselves and follow his leading voluntarily. He defends the poor man's brass and shittim-wood as no less acceptable than the rich man's abundance. Gill takes the wise-hearted for ingenious men skilled in some mechanic art, identifies what each name in the inventory covers — the tabernacle being not the whole structure but the ten fine linen curtains, the incense altar the golden altar, the pins the fastenings of the curtain-ends against the wind — and offers two senses for the cloths of service, wrappings for the vessels when the camp moved or the vestments the priests served in; he also notes that none but the willing were so much as asked.

Henry admires the speed of the response, since they went to their tents at once and did not ask time to consider, lest their zeal cool with delay; and observes that since the spoil came by special providence, it was highly fit they should devote part of it to the God they owed it all to. From the willing-hearted being singled out he infers that some were not, who loved their gold better than their God and are for the true religion provided it be cheap. He will not have the poor discouraged: those who had no precious stones brought goats' hair and rams' skins, God requiring according to what a man has, two mites from a pauper pleasing him more than talents from a Dives. On the ornaments he notes that even the women parted with bracelets and rings, preferring the beautifying of the sanctuary to their own adorning.

Clarke guesses that the cloths of service were aprons and towels, distinct from the robes of Aaron; renders the phrase about the stirred heart literally, that the heart was lifted up and the affections set on the work; and takes the last of the four ornaments for a girdle supporting the breasts. Wesley finds the motive in love to God, gratitude for what he had done and faith in what he had promised.

Ellicott agrees that some hearts did not stir them, though all classes came and gave to the utmost of their power, so that the people had at last to be restrained; and against Clarke he holds that the last of the four ornaments cannot mean tablets, coming from a root for roundness and standing most likely for a bead necklace of the Egyptian kind.

25.pericope_label: The women spin, the rulers bring the stones, and the master-workmen are named

schools.summary: Gill places the spinners socially, as the common sort of women, the richer having already been named as bringing jewels of gold; calls the stones to be set stones of fillings, filling their ouches as a stone fills a ring; and says the spices and oil were of a quality the common people had not. Calvin makes the appointment of the master-workmen an encouragement to the people, who could now see that God presided over the work, since excellent artificers though the two had been already, they were endowed further, even to a miracle. He thinks the tribe of each is named because so conspicuous a grace deserved remembering in all generations, and that God declares the names glorious in heaven of those who employ the Spirit's gifts in building his spiritual temple; that such talent survived at all in a people so long enslaved he takes for proof that these endowments were neither natural nor got by industry. Of the teaching he gives the practical reason, that two men could never have finished so arduous a work in their lifetime, and treats the patience it required as itself a gift, since otherwise the fatigue of instructing the ignorant would have defeated them; and by wisdom of heart he would have us understand activity of mind, the heart standing in Scripture not only for the affections but for the understanding.

Henry reads the naming of the master-workmen as a piece of order: it prevented strife over the office and gave everyone employed someone to take direction from, God being the God of order; and those he called by name he filled with his Spirit, skill even in secular employments being his gift. The work was extraordinary, so the man was qualified extraordinarily — as the apostles, appointed master-builders of the gospel tabernacle, were filled with the Spirit in wisdom and understanding. He adds that they were appointed not only to devise but to work, since many are ingenious at cutting out work for other people but will not touch with one finger the burdens they bind on others, and fall under the character of slothful servants; and that Bezaleel had not only power to command but a charge to instruct, so that those who rule should teach, and those to whom God gives knowledge should not covet to monopolize it.

Clarke observes that the women had learned the art of spinning before and now practised it, God condescending to accept their service, and calls the tool simple — the plain distaff or twirling pin, made of any wood they met with in the wilderness. Standing back from the whole scene he notes that the men worked and brought offerings, the women spun and brought their ornaments, and the rulers delivered up their jewels, so that all joined in the service. Wesley repeats Henry's point, that an extraordinary work required an extraordinary qualifying.

Ellicott takes wise-hearted to mean only that the women had sufficient skill, notes that the sanctuary's fabrics seem to have used flax and goats' hair alone with the flax dyed before spinning, and would render the material not fine linen but white, most Egyptian linen being a yellowish white from flax imperfectly blanched; on the second group he holds with Gill that a harder task is meant, a thread being more difficult to draw from goats' hair than from flax. He identifies the rulers with the princes of the tribes, so that the twelve stones of the breastplate would naturally be given by the chiefs whose names they were to bear, and the ephod's two onyx stones by such as owned stones of that size. Keil adds that the precious stones and the spices came from the princes, in whose hands such costly things were, and finds in the grammar that the putting into the heart to teach qualified Bezaleel to instruct workmen to prepare the articles under his own eye.

debates.question: Why is the gift described as extraordinary rather than natural skill?

sides.position: because the work itself was extraordinary, so the workman was qualified extraordinarily, as the apostles were for the gospel tabernacle
because such talent could not have survived naturally in a people so long enslaved, so the endowment was neither native nor acquired by industry

themes: all the women that were wise hearted did spin
the Lord hath called by name Bezaleel

34.pericope_label: Bezaleel and Aholiab given the gift of teaching

schools.summary: Gill treats the gift of teaching as a separate endowment from the gift of skill. God had already given Bezaleel wisdom, understanding and knowledge, enough to devise a curious work, to contrive the manner of it and to know how it should be performed; what is added here is a capacity for instruction and an inclination of the mind towards it, so that his craft should pass into other hands, others being grounded in the very matters of which he had been given understanding. The two do not always go together, since not every man of learning has either the aptitude or the appetite to pass it on, and where they do go together the second is as much of God as the first. He reads the filling with wisdom of heart the same way, the phrase meaning wisdom in their heart and the participle marking a large rather than an ordinary allowance, since whatever discernment a man has, in things natural, civil, moral or spiritual, comes from God and from nowhere else. The trades named he matches to the work each was wanted for: the engraver because stones had to be set in the ephod and breastplate, the cunning workman for the curtains, for the vail dividing the holy place from the holy of holies, and again for the ephod and breastplate, the embroiderer in blue and purple and scarlet and fine linen for the furnishings and for the dress of those employed about them, and the weaver in linen and woollen alike, the one for the curtains and hangings and the other for the priests' garments; the closing clause he extends past the crafts already named to any curious workmanship in gold, silver, brass, timber or stone.

themes: he hath put in his heart that he may teach
the engraver, the cunning workman, the embroiderer, the weaver
